text: András Hodanics / Age: 29
Rank/Position: Corporal (junior non-commissioned officer), squad leader
Civilian Occupation: Mason
Origin: Bácska / Southern Hungary (Vojvodina)
Hodanics András would have paid a serious sum —
if he'd ever possessed the kind of money that deserves the word “serious” —
for someone to explain to him how the hell he ended up here.
He knew every step of the road to the Don, obviously.
He could recite it half-asleep. The medical exam in Sombor.
The training after that in Baja. The endless train ride to the East. And the final, soul-crushing march
into the Big Nowhere that crowned the whole ordeal.
So the logistics made sense to him. What didn't make sense was the “why”. Why he had to stand here
and kill men he didn't even know? Men who had lived half a world away from him.
Men who, for all he could tell, were just as clueless about the point of this entire ordeal as he was.
He vaguely remembered that some powerful country
had attacked another, less powerful country,
and that the leaders of other, more powerful countries hadn't liked it.
But how that chain of events led to him putting down his mason's trowel
to pick up a rifle instead…
that remained a mystery to him.
Maybe it didn't even matter.
Maybe it was a waste of thought. But he just couldn't stop.
He had been a sensitive boy his whole life.
Not the kind who threw around big words,
but the kind who couldn't help wondering
what human dignity is measured in.
though he pretended otherwise in front of others.
That sensitivity
had been a handicap for as long as he could remember,
because as the mason son of a mason family
he couldn't afford that kind of frailty.
Not openly, at least. In the pub he had to take his share
of the brawls, just like his friends,
and at the pig slaughter he had to grip the knife as hard as his uncle
or any of his cousins.
So why now — an enemy of war in principle, a man who hates the very idea of it —
why does he clutch the barrel of his rifle the way a drowning man clutches a rope?
Because, after years and years of searching, he had finally found someone
in front of whom he didn't have to pretend. Someone who could accept him as he was.
And to get back to that person,
he first had to trample his own values into the mud.
He had to put down at least as many Soviets
as the bricks he had once stacked proudly, building a house for the woman he loved.
That's how he met her.
She had asked him, together with her husband,
to build them a house in the center of his hometown.
Hodanics András took the job.
Of course he did —
a long-term contract and good pay is the one-man mason's favorite combination.
Only those gray,
almost transparent eyes wouldn't let him rest —
the eyes Elza looked him over with at their first meeting,
the eyes that saw right through him.
At first he told himself he was only imagining the woman's
interest in him, but then, a few months after the job began,
summer arrived and he was baking outside in the sun,
and Elza stepped out from the neighboring house where she lived with her husband's parents,
brought him cold beer, and took a teasing sip from it herself,
while they talked about all sorts of worldly things,
things András perhaps found a little over his head.
Those conversations began in awkwardness,
but before he knew it, András found himself
opening up to her the way he never had to anyone.
Trying to seduce a married woman would have been dangerous,
and András probably didn't have the stomach for it either,
but Elza's husband had been dragged off to training a year before him,
and a few months later
the letter came: he was dead, he wasn't coming home.
Elza mourned her late husband, of course, but András saw that it wasn't with the devotion
and feeling a fresh widow ought to show.
He took it as a good sign for their future together, but even so,
out of decency he wanted to wait
for the grim weeks and months of mourning to pass,
but the war didn't adjust itself to him.
Things beyond him, things that grew over his head,
reached into the cycle of his life
and the whim of fate tossed him here, to the end of the earth.
Hodanics András aims, asks the Almighty for forgiveness,
then squeezes the trigger, and afterward shifts from one foot to the other,
because he's afraid the ring hidden in his underwear,
the one his mother gave him, the one he has carried nearly two thousand kilometers,
the one he means to use to ask Elza to marry him,
will slip down along his thigh and end up on the frozen,
blood-red ground covered in ice.
